title: Validating Input and Reporting Errors
summary: Check every request at the edge, decide between 400, 409, and 422, and answer every error in one Problem Details format.
intro: Everything a client sends is just text, and some of it is wrong: a typo, a phone app two versions behind, a script written in a hurry, and now and then a person poking for weaknesses. An API that trusts what arrives ends up storing a booking for minus five people, crashing on a date it can't read, or answering with an error so vague nobody can fix their request. This lesson shows you how to check every request where it enters, with a schema for each body and query string, where each kind of check belongs, and which status code each failure earns. Then it gives every error one shape, the Problem Details format, built in one central place in FastAPI.

steps.title: Never trust input
steps.body:
Your server can't see who is on the other end. A request from Roombook's own web app looks just like one typed into curl, and anyone can type into curl. So every part of a request, its path, query string, headers, and body, is input from outside, and could be anything at all. It goes wrong in two ways:

- **Wrong by mistake**: a misspelled field, a date in the wrong format, a number sent as text, an end time before the start, or a client built against last year's version of the API.
- **Hostile on purpose**: a fifty-megabyte body, a note of a million characters, an id of `-1` or `99999999999999999999`, or a field nobody should be able to set, like `"isAdmin": true`, or `"status": "confirmed"` on a booking that broke the rules.

## Parse at the edge

The answer is to check everything in one place: the **edge** of your API, where requests come in, before any of your own code uses them. Picture a line drawn around your server's code, called the **trust boundary**. Outside the line is text from strangers. Inside are values your code can rely on.

```diagram validation-and-errors-trust
Text from outside is checked once, at the boundary, and only typed values go further in.
```

Crossing the line is the job of **parsing**: turning text into typed values, or refusing. A parser for a booking doesn't just answer yes or no. It hands back a booking whose `attendees` is a whole number from 1 to 30, whose times are real moments in UTC, and which has no fields nobody expected. Code inside the line takes that value and never checks those things again. The idea has a slogan: **parse, don't validate**. Checking the text and then passing the text on leaves every later function wondering whether it was checked. Passing on the parsed value makes the checking part of the type.

A **schema** is how you describe a valid input: each field, its type, whether it's required, and its limits. A schema library reads a request against it and gives back either the typed value or a list of everything that's wrong.

## Why Python's type hints don't do this

Python's type hints are notes for your editor, your type checker, and the people reading the code. Python itself ignores them when it runs. Annotating `data: BookingIn`, where `BookingIn` is a `TypedDict`, changes nothing about what `data` actually holds.

FastAPI is different from plain Python here, because it reads the type hints on an endpoint's parameters and runs Pydantic on them, the schema library from Your First FastAPI Project. That's exactly the parsing this lesson is about, and most of it comes free. But FastAPI can only do it for parameters it can see. Read the body yourself with `await request.json()`, and nothing is checked at all, as the example shows.

examples.title: A handler that trusts its input
examples.prompt: This endpoint reads `data: BookingIn = await request.json()` and answers with `{"id": 1001, **data}`. Send it nonsense.
examples.explanation: Every field came back exactly as sent, and the status was 201 Created. The room id is a name, the start time is the word `whenever`, there are minus five people, and the client has quietly made itself an admin. The `TypedDict` annotation changed nothing, because Python doesn't check annotations when it runs. A real endpoint would now store this, and the bug would surface later, far from its cause. The fix is to let FastAPI see the body: declare it as a parameter with a Pydantic model for its type, and FastAPI parses it before your code runs.

steps.title: Schemas for request bodies
steps.body:
A booking request says which room, when it starts and ends, and how many people are coming, with an optional note. Here is everything its schema checks, and why:

- **Required fields and types**: `roomId` and `attendees` are whole numbers, `startsAt` and `endsAt` are times, and `note` is text or absent.
- **Formats**: times are written in **RFC 3339**, the standard text form of a date and time that JSON APIs use, like `2026-10-05T14:00:00Z` or `2026-10-05T16:00:00+02:00`. A time without an offset from UTC is refused, since `14:00` alone means a different moment in every time zone.
- **Ranges and lengths**: `roomId` is positive, `attendees` is 1 to 30, the most any room holds, and `note` is at most 500 characters. Limits like these protect the server as much as the data. A note with no limit invites someone to store a megabyte of text in every booking.
- **No unknown fields.** A client that sends `notes` instead of `note` learns about its typo at once, instead of wondering why the note never saved. A client that tries to set `status` or `userId` itself is told no, instead of having its field quietly kept, or quietly dropped.
- **Rules across fields**: `endsAt` must be after `startsAt`. That needs nothing but the request itself, so the schema can check it.

## Normalize on the way in

Parsing can also tidy what it accepts, so the rest of the code only ever sees one form of each value. This is called **normalizing**. Roombook trims spaces from the ends of the note, and converts both times to UTC, so `16:00+02:00` and `14:00Z` become the same moment. From the authentication lesson on, emails are lowercased the same way.

In FastAPI, the schema is a Pydantic model. Roombook's request models build on two base classes in `app/schemas.py`: `CamelModel`, from the lesson on request data, and `InputModel`, which adds two rules for anything a client sends:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic.alias_generators import to_camel


class CamelModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(alias_generator=to_camel, validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True)


class InputModel(CamelModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", str_strip_whitespace=True)
```

`CamelModel` gives each field its camelCase name in JSON, as before, so `room_id` in Python is `roomId` on the wire. `extra="forbid"` refuses unknown fields, and `str_strip_whitespace=True` trims every string. Pydantic merges a subclass's `model_config` with its parent's, so `InputModel` keeps the camelCase names. Here is the create model, `BookingCreate`, in `app/bookings/schemas.py`, grown from the one the lesson on request data started:

```python
class BookingCreate(InputModel):
    room_id: Annotated[StrictInt, Field(gt=0)]
    starts_at: AwareDatetime
    ends_at: AwareDatetime
    attendees: Annotated[StrictInt, Field(ge=1, le=30)]
    note: Annotated[str | None, Field(max_length=500)] = None

    @field_validator("starts_at", "ends_at")
    @classmethod
    def to_utc(cls, value: datetime) -> datetime:
        return value.astimezone(UTC)

    @field_validator("ends_at")
    @classmethod
    def after_start(cls, value: datetime, info: ValidationInfo) -> datetime:
        starts_at = info.data.get("starts_at")
        if starts_at and value <= starts_at:
            raise PydanticCustomError("time_order", "must be after startsAt")
        return value
```

- `StrictInt` refuses `"1"`. Pydantic's default is to be lenient and turn the text `"1"` into the number `1`, which hides client bugs. A model-wide `strict=True` would be simpler, but it would also refuse the time strings, because FastAPI hands Pydantic JSON that's already been decoded, where a time is still text.
- `AwareDatetime` accepts RFC 3339 times and refuses ones without an offset. The first validator converts both times to UTC, the job `UtcDatetime` did in the lesson on request data, written out here as a validator.
- The second validator sees the fields checked before it in `info.data`, so it can compare the two times and report the problem on `endsAt`. `PydanticCustomError` sets the message exactly, without the `Value error,` prefix a plain `ValueError` gets.

Declare `body: BookingCreate` on the endpoint, and FastAPI parses the body before your function runs. When it doesn't fit, FastAPI raises `RequestValidationError` with every problem, and part 6 turns that into a response.

## One schema per operation

Creating, replacing, and changing part of a booking need different schemas, even though they describe the same thing. A create requires `roomId`. A PATCH, the method from the routes lesson for changing part of a resource, can't move a booking to another room, so it has no `roomId` at all, and every field it does have is optional. Reusing the create schema for PATCH would demand fields the client didn't mean to change, and would let it send ones it mustn't. A PATCH also has to tell a field that's missing, which means leave it alone, from one sent as `null`, which means clear it, as the routes lesson pointed out.

Here is the PATCH model. Every field defaults to `None`, so the model alone can't tell a missing note from `"note": null`. As the lesson on request data showed, `body.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` holds only the fields that were sent, so a `note` key in it set to `None` means clear the note:

```python
class BookingPatch(InputModel):
    starts_at: AwareDatetime | None = None
    ends_at: AwareDatetime | None = None
    attendees: Annotated[StrictInt | None, Field(ge=1, le=30)] = None
    note: Annotated[str | None, Field(max_length=500)] = None
```

examples.title: Normalized on the way in
examples.prompt: Book Turing with a start time two hours ahead of UTC, and a note with spaces around it.
examples.code: curl -s localhost:8000/v1/bookings -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"roomId": 1, "startsAt": "2026-10-05T16:00:00+02:00", "endsAt": "2026-10-05T15:30:00Z", "attendees": 3, "note": "  Algorithms study group  "}'
examples.explanation: The request said `16:00:00+02:00`, and the stored booking says `14:00:00Z`: the same moment, now in UTC, so every later comparison, like checking for overlaps, compares like with like. The spaces around the note are gone. The rest of the booking comes from the service and the store, which the next lesson builds: an id, the user, a status, a version, and when it was created, which is the course's fixed clock. None of those were the client's to set, and the schema made sure they weren't.

examples.title: Several mistakes, one answer
examples.prompt: Send a booking with several things wrong at once.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"4 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"d55536ad-da86-47aa-8814-ac3dd1698aad","errors":[{"field":"roomId","message":"Input should be a valid integer"},{"field":"startsAt","message":"Input should be a valid datetime or date, invalid character in year"},{"field":"attendees","message":"Input should be greater than or equal to 1"},{"field":"notes","message":"Extra inputs are not permitted"}]}
examples.explanation: One answer lists all four problems: the room id was text, the start time wasn't a time, there were zero attendees, and `notes` isn't a field. The messages are Pydantic's own, and `field` uses the camelCase name the client sent, so a web app can put each message next to the right input. The rule that `endsAt` comes after `startsAt` didn't run, since `startsAt` never parsed. The shape of the whole answer, with `type`, `title`, and the rest, is part 5's subject.

steps.title: Path, query, and header values
steps.body:
Path parameters, query strings, and headers arrive as text too, and they need the same care, with two differences. Everything in them is a string, so parsing means converting text into numbers, lists, and true or false. And most of them are optional, so each needs a **default**, the value you use when the client sends none.

## Query strings

`GET /v1/rooms` takes six query parameters, and each has a rule:

| Parameter | Parsed as | Default | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| `building` | a building's slug, like `main-library` | any building | lowercase letters, digits, dashes |
| `minCapacity` | a whole number | 1 | 1 to 30 |
| `amenity` | a list, from repeated keys: `amenity=whiteboard&amenity=screen` | none | |
| `sort` | `name` or `capacity` | `name` | only those two |
| `limit` | a whole number | 20 | 1 to 100 |
| `cursor` | the opaque cursor from the last page | the first page | must be one the API issued |

Roombook refuses query parameters it doesn't know, the same as unknown body fields. A typo like `minCapcity=6` then gets a 422 naming it, instead of a full, unfiltered list that looks right.

## Bounds protect the server

A `limit` with no maximum lets one request ask for every row in the table, and a few of those at once can slow the server for everyone. So every value that controls how much work the server does gets an upper bound: page sizes, date ranges, and the length of any list. Roombook refuses `limit=500` instead of quietly lowering it to 100, so the client learns the rule instead of wondering why it got fewer rooms than it asked for.

## Cursors and ids are input too

The `nextCursor` the API hands out comes back in the next request. Clients aren't supposed to look inside one, but nothing stops them from changing it, so decode it as carefully as any other input. Roombook's cursor is base64url text holding a little JSON, so parsing it means decoding, reading the JSON, and checking that it holds a sort value and an id, and any failure is a 422 on `cursor`, never a crash.

An id in the path is different. A path that names nothing is a 404, as the routes lesson said, so `/v1/bookings/abc` gets one. Check the range too. `99999999999999999999` is digits, but it doesn't fit in the 64-bit integer the database uses for ids, so it can't name a booking either, and it's a 404 as well.

## Headers

Headers get the same treatment. The request id middleware from the middleware lesson already checks `X-Request-Id` before trusting it, and the `require_json` dependency from the lesson on request data checks `Content-Type` and answers 415. The lessons on data integrity and reliability parse `If-Match` and `Idempotency-Key` the same way: a format check, and a clear error when it fails.

The query string arrives as the `RoomQuery` model from the lesson on request data, declared with `Query()`. Here it is grown up, on the `InputModel` base, with bounds on every number and a check on the cursor, in `app/rooms/schemas.py` and `app/rooms/router.py`:

```python
class RoomQuery(InputModel):
    building: Annotated[str | None, Field(pattern=r"^[a-z0-9-]{1,40}$")] = None
    min_capacity: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=30)] = 1
    amenity: list[str] = []
    sort: Literal["name", "capacity"] = "name"
    limit: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=100)] = 20
    cursor: str | None = None

    @field_validator("cursor")
    @classmethod
    def check_cursor(cls, value: str | None) -> str | None:
        if value is not None and decode_cursor(value) is None:
            raise PydanticCustomError("cursor", "is not a cursor this API issued")
        return value
```

```python
@router.get("")
async def list_rooms(query: Annotated[RoomQuery, Query()], rooms: RoomRepositoryDep) -> Page[Room]:
```

The model gets the same `InputModel` base as the bodies, so the camelCase names, the trimming, and `extra="forbid"` all apply. A query string is always text, so here Pydantic's lenient mode is what you want: it turns `"6"` into `6` and refuses `"lots"`. `list[str]` collects repeated `amenity` keys. `decode_cursor`, from `app/pagination.py`, returns `None` for text that isn't a cursor Roombook made, so a bad cursor now joins the other field errors in one answer, instead of getting a 422 of its own from the route as it did in the lesson on request data.

For the booking id in the path, `Annotated[int, Path(gt=0, le=2**63 - 1)]` sets the type and the range. A path value that fails is still a `RequestValidationError`, and part 6 answers it with 404, not 422, since the path names nothing.

examples.title: A query string with three mistakes
examples.prompt: Ask for rooms with a capacity that isn't a number, a limit over the maximum, and a made-up cursor.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/rooms","requestId":"daf04bca-e5e5-403a-a019-0422f68ab160","errors":[{"field":"minCapacity","message":"Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer"},{"field":"limit","message":"Input should be less than or equal to 100"},{"field":"cursor","message":"is not a cursor this API issued"}]}
examples.explanation: All three problems come back at once: `lots` isn't a whole number, `500` is over the limit, and `abc` isn't a cursor the API made. The messages are Pydantic's, and `field` uses the camelCase names from the query string. The answer is the same shape as the body errors in part 2, so a client handles both with the same code. Ask for `minCapacity=5&limit=1` instead, and you get Hopper alone, the first by name of the two rooms that fit five, with a `nextCursor` for the next page.

examples.title: An id that names nothing
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking whose id isn't a number.
examples.explanation: A path that can't name a booking is a 404, the same answer as a booking id that's a number but doesn't exist. To the client, both mean there's nothing at that URL, so there's no reason to tell them apart, and no reason to say how ids are checked. The `type` is Roombook's `not-found` problem, the same for every 404.

steps.title: Where each check belongs
steps.body:
Not every check can happen at the edge. The schema knows what a booking request looks like, but not whether the Lovelace room holds five people, whether Ada already has three bookings, or whether someone booked Turing for 14:00 a second ago. Those need data, and the last one needs the database itself. So Roombook checks requests at three checkpoints:

```diagram validation-and-errors-checkpoints
Each checkpoint catches what the one before it can't, and answers with its own codes.
```

1. **The edge** checks **shape**: types, formats, ranges, required and unknown fields, and rules within the request itself. It needs nothing but the request, so it runs first and costs almost nothing. A body that can't be read at all, like broken JSON, is a **400 Bad Request**. A body in the wrong format, like text sent as `text/plain`, is a **415**. JSON that's readable but the wrong shape is a **422 Unprocessable Content**.
2. **The service**, the code that holds Roombook's business rules, which the next lesson gives its own layer, checks the rules that need data or the clock. A booking starts and ends on the hour or half past, lasts 30 minutes to 3 hours, starts in the future and at most 14 days ahead, and fits the room's capacity. And a member holds at most 3 upcoming bookings.
3. **The database** has the last word on anything two requests could race on: two bookings for the same room at the same time, or two accounts with the same email. Only the database sees every write as it happens. A check in your code reads the data and then writes, and between the two, another request can slip in. The lesson on constraints and transactions builds that rule into the database, and until then, the in-memory store plays its part.

## 400, 409, or 422

| Code | Means | Roombook examples |
|---|---|---|
| 400 Bad Request | The request can't be read at all | Broken JSON, data after the JSON value |
| 415 Unsupported Media Type | The body isn't in a format the API takes | `Content-Type: text/plain` |
| 422 Unprocessable Content | Readable, but the content breaks a rule | `attendees` of 0, an unknown field, too many people for the room |
| 409 Conflict | Fine on its own, but it clashes with data the server has now | The room is already booked, three bookings are already held |

The line between 422 and 409 takes a moment to see. Ask: would the same request succeed later, if something else changed? An overlap clears when the other booking is cancelled, and the booking limit clears when one of Ada's bookings ends. Those are conflicts, 409. Five people in a room for four is wrong no matter what anyone else does, so the request itself has to change. That's 422.

## Rules report fields too

The service's rules are about fields too, so it reports them the way the schema does: a field name and a message for each, and all of them at once. A client then handles a broken rule exactly like a broken format, with the message next to the right input.

Here are the rules in `BookingService.create`, in `app/bookings/service.py`:

```python
    async def create(self, data: NewBooking) -> Booking:
        room = await self._rooms.get(data.room_id)
        if room is None:
            raise UnprocessableError("room-not-found", "That room doesn't exist.")

        now = self._clock()
        length = data.ends_at - data.starts_at
        errors: list[FieldError] = []
        if not on_half_hour(data.starts_at):
            errors.append(FieldError("startsAt", "must be on the hour or half past"))
        if not on_half_hour(data.ends_at):
            errors.append(FieldError("endsAt", "must be on the hour or half past"))
        if not timedelta(minutes=30) <= length <= timedelta(hours=3):
            errors.append(FieldError("endsAt", "a booking lasts 30 minutes to 3 hours"))
        if data.starts_at <= now:
            errors.append(FieldError("startsAt", "must be in the future"))
        if data.starts_at > now + timedelta(days=14):
            errors.append(FieldError("startsAt", "must be at most 14 days ahead"))
        if data.attendees > room.capacity:
            errors.append(FieldError("attendees", f"{room.name} holds at most {room.capacity} people"))
        if errors:
            raise invalid_fields(errors)

        if await self._bookings.count_upcoming(data.user_id, now) >= 3:
            raise ConflictError("booking-limit", "You already have 3 upcoming bookings.")
        return await self._bookings.insert(data)
```

`UnprocessableError`, `ConflictError`, `FieldError`, and `invalid_fields` are Roombook's own, from `app/errors.py`, which part 6 introduces. A room id that names no room is its own problem, `room-not-found`. It's a 422, not a 404: the URL, `/v1/bookings`, exists, and it's the request's content that's wrong. It's checked first and alone, since without the room there's no capacity to check against. The other rules all append to `errors`, and `invalid_fields` raises them together, as one `validation-failed` error. The limit check comes only after every rule passes, since it costs a lookup in the store.

examples.title: Three broken rules
examples.prompt: Book Lovelace, which holds four, for five people, starting at a quarter past and lasting three and three quarter hours.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"51fcab01-c3c3-4b13-a5d9-3ec6890675cd","errors":[{"field":"startsAt","message":"must be on the hour or half past"},{"field":"endsAt","message":"a booking lasts 30 minutes to 3 hours"},{"field":"attendees","message":"Lovelace holds at most 4 people"}]}
examples.explanation: The body passed the schema: every field had the right type and range. Then the service found three broken rules and reported all of them, in the same shape as the schema's errors: the start isn't on the hour or half past, the booking is longer than three hours, and Lovelace holds four. It's a 422, since this request is wrong no matter what anyone else has booked. Only the request can be fixed, and the messages say exactly what to change.

examples.title: A booking that clashes
examples.prompt: With Ada's 14:00 to 15:30 booking of Turing already made, book Turing from 15:00 to 16:00.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/booking-overlap","title":"Room already booked","status":409,"detail":"The room is already booked then.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"10c64207-a49e-47d4-b831-a21ed88676de"}
examples.explanation: Every field and every rule was fine, so the request reached the store, which found the overlap with the existing booking and refused. It's a 409, with its own type, `booking-overlap`, so a client can tell it apart from every other conflict and offer to show the room's free times. The same request succeeds once the other booking is cancelled, which is what makes it a conflict and not a 422. Once the lesson on constraints and transactions moves the check into the database, the answer stays exactly the same.

steps.title: One error format: Problem Details
steps.body:
Clients have to understand your errors as well as your successes. A web app wants to show each message beside the right form field, a script wants to know whether trying again could help, and a developer wants enough to fix their request. If each endpoint invents its own error shape, every client writes special cases for each one. Roombook uses one shape for every error, the **Problem Details** format from RFC 9457, which the lesson on what an API is introduced.

## The standard members

A problem is a JSON object sent with the media type `application/problem+json`, so a client can tell an error body from a normal one by its `Content-Type` alone. RFC 9457 defines five members, all optional:

| Member | Holds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | A URI that names the kind of problem | `https://roombook.example/problems/booking-overlap` |
| `title` | A short summary of that kind, the same every time | `Room already booked` |
| `status` | The HTTP status code, repeated in the body | `409` |
| `detail` | What went wrong this time, for a person to read | `The room is already booked then.` |
| `instance` | Which occurrence it was. Roombook uses the request's path | `/v1/bookings` |

`type` is the member clients act on. Code compares the type, never the words in `title` or `detail`, which you're free to reword. So a type URI, once published, keeps its meaning for good. It doesn't have to load anything, but a page there that explains the problem is good manners. When a problem has no `type`, the RFC says to read it as `about:blank`, which means nothing beyond the status code. Roombook gives every problem a type of its own instead, so a client can always switch on `type` and never needs a fallback.

## Roombook's problem types

| `type`, after `https://roombook.example/problems/` | Status | `title` |
|---|---|---|
| `invalid-json` | 400 | Body is not valid JSON |
| `not-found` | 404 | Resource not found |
| `method-not-allowed` | 405 | Method not allowed |
| `body-too-large` | 413 | Request body too large |
| `unsupported-media-type` | 415 | Unsupported media type |
| `validation-failed` | 422 | Validation failed |
| `room-not-found` | 422 | Room not found |
| `booking-overlap` | 409 | Room already booked |
| `booking-limit` | 409 | Too many upcoming bookings |
| `internal-error` | 500 | Internal server error |
| `service-unavailable` | 503 | Service unavailable |

The database lessons add `room-name-taken`, `email-taken`, and `stale-booking`, and the authentication lesson adds its own problems, always under the same address.

## Two members of Roombook's own

The RFC lets you add members of your own, called **extension members**, and Roombook adds two:

- `requestId`, the id from the middleware lesson, on every problem, so a user can quote it and you can find the request's log lines.
- `errors`, on `validation-failed`, a list with one entry per broken field: `field`, the field's path, and `message`. A path names a field the way you'd reach it in the JSON, like `endsAt`, or `items.0.name` for a field inside a list.

Always report every field error at once. A form with three mistakes should get one answer with three errors, not three round trips that each reveal one more.

Here is how Roombook builds problems, in `app/problems.py`:

```python
TYPES = "https://roombook.example/problems/"
TITLES = {
    "invalid-json": "Body is not valid JSON",
    "not-found": "Resource not found",
    "method-not-allowed": "Method not allowed",
    "body-too-large": "Request body too large",
    "unsupported-media-type": "Unsupported media type",
    "validation-failed": "Validation failed",
    "room-not-found": "Room not found",
    "booking-overlap": "Room already booked",
    "booking-limit": "Too many upcoming bookings",
    "internal-error": "Internal server error",
    "service-unavailable": "Service unavailable",
}
BY_STATUS = {400: "invalid-json", 404: "not-found", 405: "method-not-allowed",
             413: "body-too-large", 415: "unsupported-media-type", 500: "internal-error",
             503: "service-unavailable"}


def problem(request: Request, status: int, slug: str, detail: str | None = None,
            errors: list[FieldError] | None = None, headers: dict | None = None) -> JSONResponse:
    body = {
        "type": TYPES + slug,
        "title": TITLES.get(slug, slug),
        "status": status,
        "detail": detail,
        "instance": request.url.path,
        "requestId": getattr(request.state, "request_id", None),
        "errors": [{"field": e.field, "message": e.message} for e in errors or []] or None,
    }
    body = {k: v for k, v in body.items() if v is not None}
    return JSONResponse(body, status, headers=headers, media_type="application/problem+json")
```

`TITLES` holds each problem type's title, in one place, so every problem of a type reads the same, and `BY_STATUS` names the type for the plain HTTP errors. `problem()` builds every problem the app sends. It adds `instance` and `requestId` from the request, turns the field errors into JSON, drops members that are `None`, and sets the media type on the `JSONResponse`.

steps.title: Central error handling

examples.title: Broken JSON
examples.prompt: Send a body that stops halfway through.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/invalid-json","title":"Body is not valid JSON","status":400,"detail":"The body couldn't be parsed as JSON.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"46f59847-8141-461d-b4a4-16a8916b342e"}
examples.explanation: FastAPI couldn't decode the body and raised `RequestValidationError` with a `json_invalid` error, which the first handler turned into the `invalid-json` problem. It's a 400, not FastAPI's default 422, because there's no content to judge: the server couldn't read the request at all.

examples.title: A crash, answered safely
examples.prompt: Ask for a test route whose handler fails with `connection to the database was lost`.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:35 GMT
server: uvicorn
x-request-id: a1ddd0b3-d46c-414a-92fc-630dcf56d9d8
content-length: 262

{"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/internal-error","title":"Internal server error","status":500,"detail":"Something went wrong on our side. Quote the request id if you report it.","instance":"/v1/crash","requestId":"a1ddd0b3-d46c-414a-92fc-630dcf56d9d8"}
examples.explanation: The client gets the generic `internal-error` problem and the request id, in the body and in the `x-request-id` header the handler added, and not a word about the database. The server's terminal has the rest: the JSON line with the same request id, and the traceback. Anyone who reports the error can quote the id, and whoever fixes it can find those lines in seconds.

examples.title: The 413 that skips your handlers
examples.prompt: Send a 200 KB body, over the app's `max_body_size` of 100,000 bytes.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 413 Content Too Large
date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:35 GMT
server: uvicorn
content-length: 17
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Content Too Large
examples.explanation: The status is right, 413, but the body is plain text, and there's no `x-request-id`. curl sent a `Content-Length` header, so Starlette knew the body was too big before reading it, and its body-limit middleware answered by itself, replacing any response the app tried to send. A body sent without a length is counted as it arrives, and goes through your handlers as a normal `HTTPException`. Clients should handle a 413 by its status, which is a good habit for every status anyway.

recap:
- Every part of a request is untrusted text, so parse it at the edge into typed values, and pass only those inward.
- Python's type hints aren't checked when the code runs, so Pydantic checks what actually arrives.
- A schema checks types, formats, ranges, and lengths, refuses unknown fields, and normalizes values, like times to UTC.
- Each operation gets its own schema, since create, replace, and patch need different fields.
- Query and path values are text too: convert them, give them defaults, and bound anything that costs the server work.
- Shape is checked at the edge, business rules in the service, and races in the database.
- 400 means unreadable, 422 means readable but invalid, and 409 means valid but in conflict with current data.
- Every error is a Problem Details object with a stable type, built in one central handler, and a 500 never reveals internals.
